title: Chinese Academics Begin Questioning Who Owns the Batanes Islands
author: Benjamin Koh
summary: A University Symposium, a Deleted Web Page, and the Landmass That Commands the Luzon Strait
body:
The northern archipelago that forms the anchor of Manila’s EEZ claims east of Taiwan. Beijing may be laying informational conditions to contest Philippine control over these islands. At a June 30 symposium hosted at Guangzhou’s Jinan University, several Chinese scholars asserted the islands have historically been “affiliated” with Taiwan and therefore belong to the People’s Republic of China, reports the Institute for the Study of War. The PRC-state-owned tabloid, the Global Times, touted their assertions as fact.

These scholars contended that the Philippines had no claim of sovereignty over the islands since the 1898 Treaty of Paris - under which Spain ceded the Philippines to the U.S. - excluded them from the definition of Philippine territory. They omitted that the subsequent 1900 Treaty of Washington later rectified that omission. Jinan University convened this forum to counter a May 28 Philippines-Japanese announcement of efforts to delimit overlapping EEZ claims in the Pacific, which rely upon the Batanes as the defining point of a Philippine EEZ east of Taiwan.

The approach follows China’s precedent for establishing maritime claims. The Global Times has previously published academic discussions contesting Japanese sovereignty over the Ryukyu Islands, and Beijing has used its claim of the Japanese-administered Senkaku Islands to justify sustained coast guard patrols around them. The PRC could be paving the way to establish maritime patrols around the Batanes islands under the guise of “law enforcement.” The Chinese have not formally challenged Philippine sovereignty and the website for Jinan University’s symposium was subsequently removed after international criticism - but the material remained posted elsewhere, including on the Global Times.

Geography makes these islands important. Situated on the Luzon Strait, the Batanes would form the crucial point of breakthrough for any People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) incursion beyond the first island chain. The U.S. and Philippine military forces have practiced demonstrating an ability to close the strait using area-denial weapons deployed to the islands, and Chinese authorities are concerned about the risk of being trapped in the first island chain with their surface fleet.

Establishing a regular presence in the islands could undermine Philippine control of this key maritime choke point.

The narrative of the Batanes is also another example of China’s broader use of a legal-warfare toolkit. Beijing has recently increased the number of Taiwanese individuals who are missing or detained in mainland China, following the latest in a series of intimidatory campaigns related to the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) United Front work - a point raised by ISW - after the recent implementation of a new PRC “ethnic unity law” and a July 6th assault on a Japanese-Taiwanese dual national in Taiwan which Taipei suspects could have been a foreign-directed intimidation act.

This is how a maritime claim begins: through footnoted essays and state media pronouncements rather than by a coast guard cutter. This cycle begins not with direct acknowledgment of a claim but by planting the seed of doubt. This precedent of Chinese claims is that scholars write it, media report it, Beijing neither confirms nor denies, then a patrol follows.

Beijing is seeking to make this argument, but it wants to retain its deniability.

Beijing clearly is unwilling to give up its claim of historical precedent to these islands for free. Beijing has proven willing to compromise with any challenge to China’s historical claims to territory of others for money.
